title: On this day in space! Nov. 4, 2015: A rail-launched Super Strypi rocket carrying 13 baby satellites failed during its debut launch for the US Air Force
content:
On November 4, 2015, the United States Air Force attempted a debut launch of the experimental Super Strypi rocket from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii. The rail-launched vehicle was designed to carry small payloads into orbit, marking a modern evolution of the 1960s Strypi sounding rocket. The mission intended to place 13 tiny satellites, known as cubesats, into space, but the launch failed less than a minute after liftoff.

The rocket lifted off at approximately 9:45 p.m. local time on November 3, 2015, but quickly spun out of control and crashed. The failure likely resulted from a problem with the first-stage motor and destroyed all 13 cubesats aboard. The primary payload was the ORS-4 satellite, also nicknamed HiakaSat, which was built by engineers at the University of Hawaii for the Air Force to capture Earth imagery and monitor the environment. The remaining 12 payloads included eight cubesats for NASA’s Edison Demonstration of Smallsat Networks mission and four additional university payloads.

Super Strypi was a three-stage rocket powered by Aerojet Rocketdyne solid rocket motors, designed to reach orbit rather than suborbital trajectories. The Air Force hoped the system would serve as a tool for quick-response launches based on national security needs, capable of launching up to 300 kilograms of payload for $15 million per mission. Following the 2015 failure, the program never recovered, and the Air Force did not attempt another launch with this rocket.

In the years since the failure, the U.S. Space Force has shifted its strategy for fast-turnaround launch support to commercial companies. In June of this year, the Space Force partnered with Rocket Lab to launch the Victus Haze mission with only 17 hours of notice, setting a new record for short-turnaround launch response.
summary: On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force planned to launch an experimental rocket for small satellites from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii.

title: VIB and KU Leuven find ASPM mutations disrupt neural stem cells, causing microcephaly
content:

This disruption causes microcephaly, a condition defined by an abnormally small brain and head, which is frequently accompanied by intellectual disability. The findings, published in Developmental Cell, clarify the specific mechanisms behind this developmental failure.

The study also highlights how variations in brain development render humans more susceptible to certain genetic conditions than other mammals. By uncovering these distinct developmental pathways, the research provides insight into the unique vulnerability of the human brain to ASPM gene mutations.
summary: Researchers at VIB and KU Leuven have uncovered how mutations in the ASPM gene disrupt the development of neural stem cells that help the human brain grow. title: Shockwave therapy likely cuts short‑term frozen‑shoulder pain, long‑term benefit unclear
content: A recent review of the latest trial evidence published by The BMJ reports that extracorporeal shockwave therapy probably reduces short‑term pain associated with frozen shoulder. The review also finds that manipulation under anesthesia—whether combined with steroid injections or not—probably improves short‑term flexion compared with usual care.
summary: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy probably reduces short‑term pain associated with frozen shoulder. Manipulation under anesthesia, with or without steroid injections, probably improves short‑term arm flexion compared with usual care, according to a BMJ review of recent trial evidence.

title: Study: Unfortified plant-based dairy swaps may cause nutrient deficiencies
content: A new study from the University of Surrey reports that replacing dairy products, even partially, with unfortified plant-based alternatives may lead to deficiencies in vital nutrients. The research suggests that mandatory fortification of these plant-based alternatives and other foods, such as bread, could lessen the risk of such deficiencies, particularly iodine deficiency.
summary: A University of Surrey study reports that replacing dairy with unfortified plant-based alternatives may lead to deficiencies in vital nutrients. The researchers suggest that mandatory fortification of these products and other foods could reduce the risk of such deficiencies.

content: U.S. experts warn in The BMJ that fireworks pose an underestimated danger to public health. They recommend implementing stronger regulations and sustained public education campaigns to prevent devastating yet entirely avoidable injuries.

content: A new study led by investigators at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center suggests that routine breast imaging, such as mammograms, may offer little benefit to women who have undergone a double mastectomy. The research focuses on patients treated for ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), a noninvasive form of breast cancer also known as stage 0 breast cancer.

content: New Stanford Medicine-led research indicates that specific brain firing patterns in cognitively normal adults can predict Alzheimer's disease years before memory loss or the accumulation of plaques and tangles. The study also found that distinct firing patterns in other individuals signal unusual resilience to cognitive decline, suggesting a trajectory toward "super ager" status.
summary: New Stanford Medicine-led research found that specific brain firing patterns in cognitively normal adults can predict Alzheimer's disease years before memory loss occurs. Other distinct firing patterns indicated unusual resilience to cognitive decline and a trajectory toward super ager status.

This finding highlights a significant gap in the medical response to youth vaping, indicating that many doctors are unequipped to direct teens toward appropriate cessation resources.
summary: New Federation University research indicates that two-thirds of Australian pediatricians do not know where to refer adolescents for vaping cessation support. This finding highlights a critical gap in the medical response to youth vaping.

content: Scientists have identified how cosignaling receptors dually regulate T cell activation through phase separation. While prior research established that the T cell receptor (TCR) undergoes phase separation with the kinase Lck to mediate rapid activation upon antigen stimulation, the specific mechanism by which costimulating receptors influence this process had previously remained unclear.

content: University of Sydney researchers have directly observed hydrogen dissolved in the minute gaps between atoms within metal alloys. This world-first observation of hydrogen in metal crystal lattices provides new insights into how hydrogen weakens metals and could aid in the development of more hydrogen-resistant materials.
summary: Researchers at the University of Sydney have directly observed hydrogen dissolved in the tiny gaps between atoms in metal alloys. The world‑first observation offers fresh insight into why hydrogen can weaken metals and may help develop more hydrogen‑resistant materials.

title: Brazil ranchers on Dirty List bypass forced labor rules via intermediaries
content:
Brazil’s "Dirty List," a public registry identifying employers who violated anti-slavery laws, remains a central tool in the country’s fight against forced labor. Major meatpackers have committed to sustainable sourcing by refusing to buy cattle directly from ranchers named on this list. However, new research indicates that these safeguards are being circumvented. Ranchers on the list are rerouting their cattle through intermediaries, effectively bypassing the direct purchase restrictions.

This practice allows cattle associated with forced labor to continue moving through domestic and international beef and leather supply chains. The findings suggest that the current sourcing commitments are insufficient to prevent the exploitation of workers, as the use of middlemen obscures the origin of the livestock from the meatpackers.
summary: New research indicates that Brazilian ranchers on the anti-slavery Dirty List reroute cattle through intermediaries to avoid direct sales restrictions. This practice allows cattle linked to forced labor to remain in domestic and international beef and leather supply chains.
author: Phys.org

title: European orbiter detects fresh hints of volcanic activity on Mars
content: New data from a European orbiter suggests Mars may still possess internal geological activity. Gas seeping above volcanic rifts in the Alba Mons region indicates that fresh fissures could be allowing gases from the planet’s interior to reach the surface, challenging the notion that Mars is geologically dead.
summary: New evidence from gas seeping above volcanic rifts suggests Mars is not geologically dead but merely sleeping. Fresh fissures along the Alba Mons region hint at active spots where gases from inside the planet may be reaching the surface.

title: Earth atmosphere emulators could enable faster and more accurate weather predictions
content: Partitioning the Earth from just below the surface to the top of the atmosphere into 1-kilometer-square chunks results in billions of cells. Running these cells through complex physics equations allows the entire Earth system to interact and evolve in detail, one step at a time.
summary: Dividing the Earth system into 1-kilometer-square chunks requires running billions of cells through complex physics equations. This detailed simulation allows the entire Earth system to interact and evolve step by step.

title: New Theoretical Route for Calculating Gluon Production in Proton-Nucleus Collisions
content: Theoretical studies of proton-nucleus collisions describe colliding projectiles as streams of color charges moving along specific trajectories. These charges couple to gluons, which subsequently generate the particles observed in the final state, including gluons and quarks that eventually form hadrons.
summary: Theoretical studies describe colliding projectiles in proton-nucleus collisions as streams of color charges moving along their trajectories. These color charges couple to gluons, which produce the final-state particles observed as gluons, quarks, and hadrons.

content: A close examination of a frequently visited cave wall in Spain has revealed a spectacular assembly of rock‑art engravings that researchers believe are at least 19,000 years old. The discovery highlights the cave’s significance as a site of prehistoric art.

title: Gauge open-sources CLI to recursively improve docs for coding agents
content:
Evan from Gauge has announced the open-sourcing of a command-line interface (CLI) designed to recursively improve documentation for coding agents. The tool includes a local execution backend, allowing users to try it without creating an account. An explainer video is available to demonstrate the functionality, and the project is hosted on GitHub with installation instructions provided via npm.

The CLI operates on a "hillclimbing loop" designed to optimize agent-facing surfaces such as documentation, Skills, and CLIs. The process involves setting up tasks for coding agents, running those tasks, and analyzing session transcripts to identify friction or failures. Users then create variants of their documentation to resolve these issues and re-run the tasks with the new variants injected transparently at the same hostname. This cycle repeats until a variant successfully resolves the identified problems.

The system’s architecture consists of two main components: virtual machines and a network gateway. The VMs are designed to be highly privileged to accurately represent developers' coding agents, typically containing the agent harness, language toolchains, and a git repository. The network gateway terminates TLS connections and swaps in documentation variants while handling credential replacement. This ensures that agents see placeholders for credentials and cannot exfiltrate keys. For local execution, the CLI uses Docker containers for VMs and runs mitmproxy in a sidecar container for each session to manage the network gateway.

Gauge stated that they began two years ago building open-source developer tools, including Tach, before pivoting to AI Search optimization and now focusing on the intersection of both fields. The team noted that devtool companies they worked with were the first to ask how to optimize for Claude Code and Codex. The CLI provides primitives for documentation, developer relations, and engineering teams to measure and improve how coding agents utilize their products.

The team has used the hillclimbing loop internally to fix issues such as mistaken pricing, inaccurate product limitations, and repeated workarounds. They identified that coding agents incorrectly reported Gauge only supported Claude Code and Codex, traced this to specific web pages, and corrected the documentation to include support for Pi, OpenCode, and Antigravity. Additionally, Gauge assisted Clerk in shifting coding agents from a legacy "keyless" mode to a new "clerk init" command. After validating a pre-release change to SDK error messages using the tool, Clerk observed a threefold increase in coding agents using the "clerk init" command post-deployment.

The developers argue that the static nature of AI models enables closed-loop optimization for software products, as the same agent can be simulated repeatedly in a high-fidelity testing environment. They emphasize that achieving optimal results requires high-quality analysis to find generalizable friction and paired experiments that vary only the content to measure downstream behavioral changes. The post invites feedback from the Hacker News community on whether this approach improves upon DIY or in-house solutions and what changes might be necessary.
summary: Gauge has open-sourced a CLI that uses a hillclimbing loop to analyze session transcripts and create doc variants to resolve coding agent friction. The tool includes a local execution backend using Docker containers and a network gateway to transparently swap in documentation variants during testing.

title: PopSocket phone grip with butter design sparks user enthusiasm
content:
The Verge’s Allison Johnson shares her experience adopting a phone grip, comparing the initial attraction to finding a great recipe. The story begins with a friend’s new accessory, a PopSocket-branded combo featuring a phone case with bold stripes and a grip designed to look like a stick of butter. Labeled "unsalty" and complete with tablespoon markings, the accessory was a playful nod to the current trend of butter-themed items, a fact Johnson learned from a 12-year-old friend.

Johnson describes becoming enamored with the friend’s eye-catching setup, which led her to order a similar grip for herself a few weeks later. This purchase marked a shift in her personal style, as she had previously favored buttoned-up, minimalist technology. The article details her journey from a minimalist approach to embracing a more expressive and whimsical tech accessory.
summary: A user adopted a PopSocket phone grip designed to look like a stick of butter after seeing a friend use it. The accessory features "unsalty" labeling and tablespoon markings, contrasting with the user's previous minimalist tech style.

title: 17 better ways Elon Musk could have wasted $446 million
content:
Elon Musk’s America PAC spent $446 million on midterm elections, a sum the article describes as a delusional waste of nearly $500 million. The piece critiques social media’s influence, suggesting that excessive engagement with attention-seeking posts can lead to such financial missteps.

Specifically, $47 million from the PAC was directed at defeating Texas Democrat James Talarico. However, Talarico defeated Musk’s preferred Senate candidate, Ken Paxton, securing 55 percent of the vote. The article notes that Talarico even made Musk’s influence a central part of his campaign.

title: Qualcomm targets $15B data center revenue by 2029 as smartphone sales decline
content:
Qualcomm is pivoting toward the AI data center market to offset a 20 percent decline in smartphone sales compared to 2025. During its Q4 2026 earnings call, the company detailed plans to expand this business segment through partnerships with Amazon and Meta, which were announced earlier in the year. Management expects this new division to grow rapidly, projecting $650 million in revenue for the first quarter of 2027.

The company forecasts that data center revenue will reach $5 billion by the end of 2027 and $15 billion by 2029. These projections are significant relative to Qualcomm’s total revenue of $10.4 billion for 2026, highlighting the strategic importance of the data center sector to the firm’s future financial performance.
summary: Qualcomm is shifting focus to AI data centers to offset a 20 percent drop in smartphone sales. The company forecasts data center revenue will reach $5 billion by the end of 2027 and $15 billion by 2029.

title: Ted Cruz pushes for Republican majority on FCC before 2027 Senate shift
content:
Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is seeking to expand the Republican majority on the Federal Communications Commission before Democrats assume control of the Senate in January 2027. Cruz announced a nomination hearing for Trump’s FCC nominee, Danielle Thumann Severs, to be held on November 10, shortly after the Republicans’ midterm loss. As the chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee for his final two months, Cruz intends to advance the Thumann Severs nomination to a full Senate vote.

Confirming Thumann Severs would establish a 3-1 Republican advantage on the FCC. This majority could shift to 3-0 by the end of 2027, as FCC Democrat Anna Gomez would be required to leave the commission at that time unless Trump agrees to renominate her.
summary: Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is aiming to widen the Republican majority on the Federal Communications Commission before Democrats take over control of the Senate in January 2027. Just before the Republicans' midterm loss, Cruz yesterday announced a November 10 nomination hearing for Trump's FCC nominee, Danielle Thumann Severs.

title: Elon Musk Announces SpaceX HQ Move from California to Texas Starbase
content:
Elon Musk relocated to Texas in 2020, settling outside of Austin following public disputes with California authorities during the COVID-19 pandemic. Over the subsequent six years, he intensified his commitment to the state. In 2021, Musk directed the Starship program toward South Texas, encouraging SpaceX employees to relocate for the company’s future development. That same year, in March, he began using the name Starbase to designate the production and launch facilities situated near the Rio Grande River.

Musk continued to expand SpaceX’s presence in Texas in 2023 by constructing a massive factory east of Austin. This facility is dedicated to manufacturing customer terminals and other electronics for the Starlink program. In July 2024, he announced that SpaceX would move its corporate headquarters from Hawthorne, California, to Starbase, Texas. Musk cited California’s regulatory and political environment as the primary motivation for this corporate relocation.
summary: Elon Musk moved to Texas in 2020 after disputes with California authorities and focused the Starship program and Starlink factory there. In July 2024 he announced SpaceX would relocate its corporate headquarters from Hawthorne, California to the Starbase facility in Texas, citing California's regulatory environment.

title: Voters Pass 38 of 44 Data Center Restrictions, Slowing Trump’s AI Buildout
content: Donald Trump’s big, rapid American AI buildout now faces a major slowdown as voters in yesterday’s elections overwhelmingly supported candidates and measures that favored increasing restrictions on AI and data centers nationwide. One resource from a polling firm, called Redbud Consulting, tracked data center initiatives on the ballot and reported that out of 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers, 38 passed so far. Those measures included dozens of moratoriums and bans. Analysts suggested those won’t impact data centers already under construction or approved through 2027, instead largely impacting future projects planned for 2028. Only one measure passed allowing a data center to proceed. But even that small win represented pushback on the AI industry—requiring data center developers in a North Dakota city to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings when expanding or proposing projects. In addition to increasing regulations on data centers, voters also backed anti-AI candidates, electing officials vowing crackdowns in key states building out the most data center capacity in the US. summary: In recent elections, voters approved 38 of 44 measures aimed at restricting data centers, including moratoriums and bans. The approvals slowed Trump’s AI buildout and also led to the election of officials pledging AI industry crackdowns in key states.

title: AMD Q3 Revenue Hits $13.4B as Data Center Sales Double, Gaming Falls
content:
AMD announced third‑quarter revenues of $13.4 billion, a 45 percent increase from the same period last year. The company said its data‑center business nearly doubled, while the gaming segment declined. Chief financial officer Jean Hu noted that AMD expects revenue for the year to be roughly $17 billion, give or take 3 percent, and that the middle point of its guidance represents about 66 percent year‑over‑year growth, largely driven by the acceleration of the data‑center segment.

AMD projects fourth‑quarter revenue to rise another 27 percent from the current quarter’s results. According to Tom’s Hardware, Intel’s fourth‑quarter guidance places revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion, meaning that if both companies meet their estimates, AMD would surpass Intel’s revenue for the first time in history.

The data‑center segment grew 97 percent year over year, reaching a record $8.5 billion. AMD attributes this surge to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs and the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs. In the client business, sales of AMD Ryzen mobile chips drove growth, with desktop Ryzen processors contributing $2.95 billion in revenue, up 7 percent year over year.
summary: AMD posted third‑quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45 percent year over year, with its data center segment nearly doubling and its gaming segment falling. The company’s CFO Jean Hu said the company expects total revenue of about $17 billion for the year, a 66 percent increase driven mainly by the data center business.

title: VMware releases vSphere Express for virtualization on up to 128 cores
content:
Broadcom’s VMware has announced a new product, vSphere Express, aimed at small‑to‑medium‑sized businesses (SMBs). The offering is described as a lower‑end virtualization solution that supports up to 128 cores and is marketed as “cost‑effective essential virtualization.”

The move follows reports that many SMB customers felt pressured by VMware to adopt VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), the company’s flagship private‑cloud bundle. VCF is noted for its extensive feature set and higher cost—features that many SMBs say they do not need. In addition, some SMB users have said that VMware sales representatives previously informed them that vSphere Standard, the former entry‑level product, was no longer available. The new vSphere Express is intended to address those concerns and provide a more suitable option for smaller organizations.
summary: VMware announced vSphere Express, a lower‑end virtualization offering for organizations that require “cost‑effective essential virtualization.” The product follows reports that VMware had been pushing SMB customers toward the expensive VMware Cloud Foundation bundle and that vSphere Standard was reportedly no longer available.

title: Uranium cubes show German nuclear program lacked sufficient material
content:
A recent study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences Nexus has clarified why the Nazi German nuclear program never produced a bomb. The paper, written by a team that included University of Maryland physicist Timothy Koeth, argues that the German effort lacked the necessary uranium and heavy water to build a functioning reactor, despite claims by Werner Heisenberg that they were close to criticality with the B8 pile.

Heisenberg’s 1940s project had focused on a reactor design that, according to the new research, could not reach critical mass without additional fissile material. The paper’s analysis shows that the German supply of uranium and heavy water was insufficient for the design they were pursuing, contradicting Heisenberg’s assertion that only a small amount of extra material was needed.

Koeth’s interest in the topic began in 2013 when a friend gave him a heavy‑metal cube that he immediately identified as one of the uranium cubes used by German scientists. Only fourteen of these cubes are known to exist today. In 2019, Koeth and then‑graduate student Miriam “Mimi” Hiebert documented their search for the cubes’ origins, locating ten of them across the United States.

Among the cubes they found were a German uranium cube in storage at the Smithsonian Institution and another that had circulated through introductory physics courses at Harvard University. These artifacts provide tangible evidence of the German program’s attempts and help explain why the project ultimately failed.
summary: Uranium cubes show German nuclear program lacked sufficient material.

title: Kremlin-linked hackers exploit iOS and Android flaws to infect phones via malicious sites
content:
Hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws to target visitors of multiple websites, researchers said Wednesday. The attackers were assessed with “moderate to high confidence” as part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service. Their attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic profiled the device, and the final payloads, tailored to the platform, attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi‑Fi passwords and full mobile device data.

The researchers noted that the attackers targeted other sites, many with links to Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. One of the impersonated sites was america250.org, a domain belonging to a non‑partisan group of lawmakers, business executives, and at least one former member of the Trump administration. The attackers registered america250.holiday and used it as a reverse proxy to america250.org, delivering content from the real site that included malicious JavaScript.
summary: Kremlin-linked hackers exploit iOS and Android flaws to infect phones via malicious sites.

title: Macronix to Stop ROM Chip Production, Impacting Nintendo Switch Cartridges
content: For years, the AI industry's insatiable demand for memory and storage has had plenty of knock-on effects on the price and availability of PC components like RAM, SSDs, and GPUs. Now those shortages are also squeezing the supply of ROM chips that power physical Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 game cartridges. Chip manufacturer Macronix announced in its third-quarter earnings report that the company's production of ROM chips "has reached its end" and that it will begin "gradually decoupling from the game industry," as reported by Taiwanese news site BigGo Finance. That could be an issue for Nintendo, which analyst David Gibson notes uses Macronix as its "main memory chip maker" for physical game cartridges. That ROM production—which has shrunk 39 percent in the last year and now represents just 5 percent of Macronix's business—is being crowded out by production of more lucrative, in-demand chips like NOR- and NAND-based memory and eMMCs, the company said. With Macronix's production capacity stuck at 25,000 12-inch wafers a month—and $1.2 billion in planned new capacity taking a year or more to spin up—less profitable ROM chips are taking up wafer space that can earn more through other types of chips. Read full article Comments
summary: Macronix announced that its ROM chip production has reached its end and it will gradually decouple from the game industry. This change may affect Nintendo, which uses Macronix as its main memory chip maker for physical Switch cartridges.

title: Republican strategist Bryan Lanza says MAGA lost grip after midterm defeat
content:
Erin Ogunkeye recently introduced Bryan Lanza, a Republican strategist and partner in Mercury’s Washington, D.C. office, to discuss the recent midterm election. Lanza explained that the MAGA movement’s confrontational style had been a hallmark of the party, but the “veritable blue wave” that swept the election has sent a warning that the electorate wants a different approach.

Lanza noted that President Donald Trump has acknowledged the Democratic victory, sometimes adopting a combative tone and at other times a conciliatory one. He urged the president to use his remaining two years to reverse tariffs he calls damaging, address widespread dissatisfaction with immigration enforcement, and manage the highly unpopular Iran war.

content:
A special fact‑checking segment hosted by Vedika Bahl examines Donald Trump’s second term, focusing on three recurring tactics. The program notes that Trump continues to launch frequent attacks on political opponents and to employ AI‑generated images that portray him favorably while advancing political narratives. It also explores the responses journalists receive when they challenge his statements.

The segment references Trump’s earlier role in popularising the phrase “fake news” and observes that his presidency has been marked by numerous false claims, conspiracy theories and misleading content.
summary: Donald Trump popularized the term “fake news” and his presidency has been filled with false claims, conspiracy theories and misleading content. content: Shares of Tesla and SpaceX fell after the Democratic Party won a sweeping victory in the United States midterm elections. The crisis culminated in a breakdown of negotiations with its primary landlord, Scentre Group, the owner of Westfield.

title: Review: Marina Litvinenko's 'A Life in Fragments' reflects on surviving husband's murder
content:
Twenty years after the murder of her husband, Marina Litvinenko has published A Life in Fragments, a reflection on love and resilience. The book serves as a personal account from the widow of Russian dissident Alexander Litvinenko, who was poisoned with radioactive polonium in November 2006 after meeting visitors from Moscow. A public inquiry later concluded that Vladimir Putin had “probably” approved the assassination, which was carried out by two assassins.

Litvinenko’s deathbed image, showing him in intensive care with a defiant gaze, became a global symbol of the regime under Putin. The picture highlighted what the text describes as a cruel and vindictive post-millennial Russia, ruled by a paranoid KGB leader. Alexander Litvinenko is characterized as an ill-fated prophet who warned British detectives that he was the target of a vengeful mafia state. He had presciently cautioned that if unchecked, Putin would initiate a war resulting in millions of deaths.
summary: Marina Litvinenko's book "A Life in Fragments" reflects on love and resilience twenty years after her husband Alexander Litvinenko was murdered. A public inquiry concluded that Vladimir Putin probably approved the poisoning of Litvinenko with radioactive polonium.

title: William T Vollmann's 3,000‑page novel A Table for Fortune chronicles CIA history
content: This insider’s history of the CIA explores the last 50 years of US foreign policy with granular detail and mordant humour The 250th year of the American experiment seems to invite a reckoning. For a young country, the United States is overblessed – or burdened – with myths about its foundation and how the nation has conducted itself at home and abroad. William T Vollmann’s 3,000-page novel A Table for Fortune is an epic attempt, 15 years in the making, to engage with the US’s past and present at an institutional and a personal level. The four simultaneously published volumes offer both a family story and an insider’s history of the CIA, in order to show the consequences of the quest for liberty and the belief in American exceptionalism. Vollmann’s previous novels have explored the ideological basis of American society, most notably those of the Seven Dreams series, published from 1990 to 2015, which depict the generally disastrous encounters between American settlers and Indigenous peoples. A Table for Fortune continues this project by investigating the last 50 years of US foreign policy, at the heart of which is 9/11, with the book “tracing the roots of that crime in one direction and its poisoned harvest in another”. Though the CIA has been fertile ground for many great American novelists – Don DeLillo, Norman Mailer – Vollmann is perhaps the first to represent the culture and daily activities of the agency in granular detail. His great gambit is to frame this as a dark workplace comedy of minor resentments, sexual tension and office banter. These sections are narrated by the institutional voice of the CIA itself in a relentlessly sardonic tone rife with acronyms, codenames and jargon rendered in multiple fonts. The mordant humour of the narrator, who regards all forms of death and suffering as “ fun ”, has a seductive quality that allows Vollmann to educate the reader about a broad sweep of geopolitical subjects ranging from the Angolan civil war to the interrogation methods of the Stasi, and in doing so chart the hypocrisies and double standards of the agency.
summary: William T Vollmann's 3,000‑page novel A Table for Fortune chronicles CIA history.

title: England Rugby League Players Stuck in Australia a Week After World Cup Exit
content:
England’s men’s rugby league team is experiencing a delayed departure from the Rugby League World Cup in Australia, with some players not returning home until Friday, a week after their campaign concluded. The squad’s early exit was confirmed on Sunday during the Tonga versus Samoa match, after which the team relocated to Sydney. This prolonged stay contrasts with the England women’s team, who departed Australia the morning after their tournament was ended by Samoa.

During their time in Wollongong, the England men’s squad stayed at a hotel overlooking the local beaches, where the scent of seaweed and mist from the bay was common. The coastal location allowed some players to easily access the water and enabled those with family nearby to begin their end-of-season holidays early. Wigan teammates Junior Nsemba and Zach Eckersley spent time riding e-scooters on Cliff Road and strolling along North Beach, activities that may become significant memories of the trip alongside their matches against Tonga, France, and Papua New Guinea.

Despite the scenic surroundings, which included cafes and lilac jacaranda trees, most England players and staff expressed a strong desire to return home. The situation highlights a period of waiting for the squad, who were effectively told to leave the tournament but remained in the country for an extended period. An advertisement outside their North Bay hotel in Wollongong read, “Everything that truly matters is possible,” a sentiment that did not apply to their immediate circumstances as they waited for their final travel arrangements.
summary: England men's rugby league players will not return home until Friday, a week after their early exit from the World Cup in Australia. The squad has moved to Sydney after their campaign ended, while the women's team departed the morning after their loss to Samoa.

title: Billy Loughnane signs Godolphin retainer to ride alongside William Buick
content: The combination of prodigious talent in the saddle and an easy likeability out of it is a perfect fit for Dubai operation “I want to ride more Group One winners,” Billy Loughnane said last month when asked to name his main ambition for 2027, and Britain’s new 20-year-old champion jockey seems all but certain to achieve his aim, following Wednesday’s news that he has signed a retainer to ride in the royal blue colours of Sheikh Mohammed’s global Godolphin operation next year. Loughnane will be contracted alongside William Buick as one of two retained Godolphin jockeys next year, and not as an outright No 1, but even if Loughnane does not claim the lion’s share of the best rides as soon as next year, his trajectory within the operation seems clear.
summary: Billy Loughnane has signed a retainer to ride for Sheikh Mohammed's Godolphin operation next year. He will be contracted as one of two retained jockeys alongside William Buick.

content:
Rory McIlroy voiced support on Wednesday for DP World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings’ claim that LIV Golf aimed to “destroy” the European golf circuit. The six-time major winner and former world No 1 discussed Kinnings’ recent interview with the Scotsman while speaking with media ahead of the Abu Dhabi Championship.

Kinnings had also stated that the DP World Tour pays everyone on time, contrasting it with an “arms race” in professional golf attributed to LIV Golf.

title: Six Nations and Sanzaar agree to sell global broadcast rights together
content:
The Six Nations and Sanzaar unions have agreed to sell all media rights and commercial deals collectively under a new revenue-sharing model. This innovative arrangement, described as the first of its kind in sport, will be overseen by a new rights management agency. The deal aims to help rugby’s biggest unions grow their revenues by pooling their commercial interests.

Under the agreement, southern hemisphere nations will receive a share of profits from Six Nations and British & Irish Lions tours. Conversely, European countries will benefit from broadcast and sponsorship deals generated by the Rugby Championship and the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series between New Zealand and South Africa.
summary: The Six Nations and Sanzaar unions have agreed to sell all media rights and commercial deals collectively for the first time. This new revenue-sharing model allows southern hemisphere nations to share in Six Nations profits while European countries benefit from Rugby Championship deals.

title: RFU backs Borthwick for World Cup despite England Nations Championship struggles
content:
Steve Borthwick has received unequivocal backing from the Rugby Football Union to lead England into next year’s World Cup, regardless of the team’s performance in the upcoming autumn Nations Championship. RFU chief Bill Sweeney offered full support to the head coach, whose contract was extended in September to run through the 2028 Six Nations. This extension was implemented to prevent speculation ahead of the tournament, even though England recorded their worst Six Nations performance this year.

Despite the organizational support, Borthwick remains under pressure following five defeats in his team’s last seven matches. The squad was recently boosted by the return of fly-half Fin Smith to training, providing a potential positive development for the side as they prepare for the remainder of the autumn campaign.
summary: RFU chief Bill Sweeney has offered full support to Steve Borthwick to lead England into next year's World Cup, even if the team performs poorly this autumn. Borthwick's contract was extended in September to end after the 2028 Six Nations to avoid speculation, despite five defeats in the past seven matches.

title: US stocks jump as Democrats win Senate and House, dollar falls
content:
US investors reacted positively to the results of the midterm elections, pushing the country’s major equity indexes higher.  The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed close to 3%, its best day in more than a year, while the Nasdaq and S&P 500 each gained about 1.5% by the close on Wednesday afternoon.  

The rally followed a shift in sentiment that eased early concerns about how the election outcome might affect growth in the world’s largest economy.  Market participants expressed hope that Donald Trump’s turbulent policymaking would be restrained under a new Democratic majority in both chambers of Congress.  

At the same time, U.S. government bond yields fell, and the gains in the stock market reversed overnight declines in U.S. futures that had emerged after the news that Democrats had secured control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.
summary: US stocks surged on Wednesday, with the Dow Jones up close to 3% and the Nasdaq and S&P 500 each gaining about 1.5% after Democrats secured control of the Senate and the House. title: Geolinking Service SoRa strengthens interdisciplinary research in Germany
content:
The "Geolinking Service SoRa" research data infrastructure addresses a gap in the German research landscape by facilitating interdisciplinary analyses. This service enables the linking of social science and spatial science data, which is necessary to answer complex questions regarding social inequality and environmental justice.

Specific research inquiries supported by this infrastructure include determining if the proportion of green space in residential neighborhoods affects health and well-being. summary: The Geolinking Service SoRa research data infrastructure helps close a gap in the German research landscape by linking social science and spatial science data. title: Review in Nature Reviews Biodiversity outlines light pollution's ecological impacts

The authors note that this phenomenon disrupts biological processes at all levels, ranging from genes to entire ecosystems, and contributes significantly to global biodiversity loss.

Based on a comprehensive assessment of impacts on organisms in both terrestrial and aquatic environments, the article outlines specific priorities for future research and management. The review aims to address the widespread effects of light pollution on biological systems, providing a framework for understanding its role in environmental degradation.

title: Toothbrush that emits electricity may more effectively prevent gum disease
content:
A novel toothbrush utilizing piezoelectric bristles has demonstrated superior efficacy in reducing dental plaque and gum inflammation compared to conventional products. Developed by researchers led by Yanhui Lu at Peking University in China, the device generates electricity as its bristles bend during brushing. This mechanical action triggers the formation of reactive-oxygen species, molecules that damage bacterial membranes, while the bristles simultaneously remove plaque physically. The innovation addresses the limitation of standard brushing, which often leaves bacteria deep within plaque or between teeth, allowing colonies to regrow rapidly.

The research team created two sets of bristles with varying thicknesses, both of which adhered to Chinese national standards for softness and strength. Laboratory tests confirmed that the bristles produced electric charges under pressure, with the thicker variants showing particularly high electrical generation. The brushes retained their softness and electrical properties after three months of use. In controlled experiments involving simulated brushing movements, the thicker piezoelectric bristles killed approximately 53 per cent of Streptococcus mutans, a bacterium associated with cavities, and 78 per cent of Porphyromonas gingivalis, which contributes to gum disease. In contrast, standard nylon bristles eliminated only 9 per cent and 8 per cent of these bacteria, respectively.

Further testing involved growing plaque from human mouths on cow enamel pieces and brushing them for three minutes. The piezoelectric toothbrushes removed more than 99 per cent of the plaque, whereas conventional nylon brushes removed about 80 per cent. The study also included a clinical trial with 109 adults who had dental plaque and gum inflammation. Participants were randomly assigned to use either the piezoelectric or a nylon toothbrush twice daily for three months. Dental examinations showed that the piezoelectric group experienced reductions of roughly 40 per cent in plaque build-up, gum inflammation, and bleeding, compared to around 15 per cent for the conventional brush group.

Genetic sequencing of dental plaque from the piezoelectric user group indicated a decline in the relative abundance of harmful bacteria and an increase in some potentially beneficial bacteria. Nicholas Jakubovics, a researcher at Newcastle University in the UK who was not involved in the study, described the concept as innovative because the mechanical forces recharge the surface. He noted that any improvement in dental care methods could be beneficial given the widespread nature of oral disease, which affects nearly half the global population. Previous attempts to enhance toothbrushes have included antibacterial metal nanoparticles or battery-dependent ionic currents, but the long-term effectiveness of some of these methods remains uncertain.

The findings were published in the journal Science Advances. Jakubovics emphasized that larger studies are now required to determine whether the toothbrush effectively prevents long-term issues such as cavities and tooth loss. The research highlights a potential advancement in oral hygiene tools by leveraging piezoelectric materials, which have previously been shown to fight bacteria in infected wounds and medical implants.
summary: A new and improved toothbrush could help avoid trips to the dentist Westend61/Alamy A toothbrush that generates electricity may more effectively fight harmful bacteria, while removing plaque, than existing products. The toothbrush uses special bristles that produce electricity as they bend, triggering the formation of molecules that damage bacterial membranes.

title: Hubble Study Finds Dwarf Galaxies Retain Only Small Fraction of Stellar Oxygen
content:

Researchers utilized Hubble to examine 37 nearby dwarf galaxies, defined as small systems containing thousands to hundreds of millions of stars. The study revealed that these galaxies retain only a small fraction of the oxygen produced by their stars, leaving much of the expected oxygen missing. This finding underscores a significant cosmic mystery regarding how dwarf galaxies manage their elemental composition.
summary: Researchers using NASA's Hubble Space Telescope studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies and found that much of the expected oxygen is missing. The study, known as GLOW, revealed that these small galaxies can hold onto only a small fraction of the oxygen made by their stars.

title: NASA awards Ka-band satellite relay contracts to Astranis, Global Enterprise, Viasat
content:
NASA announced on Wednesday that it has awarded contracts to three companies to develop Ka‑band space relay capability concepts that are compatible with current missions in space. The selected firms will design solutions that maintain service continuity for existing spacecraft without requiring modifications to their onboard systems. The work is intended to deliver end‑to‑end solutions—including space, ground, launch, operations, and integration elements—as part of NASA’s broader commercial marketplace strategy.

The awards are firm‑fixed‑price contracts issued under the Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships‑3 Broad Agency Announcement Appendix E. NASA retains the option to provide additional funding, up to the award limit, to advance the projects from initial concept development and risk reduction to an in‑orbit flight demonstration. The initial period of performance runs from November 4 through May 3, 2027, with priced options that could extend the work through 2029.

The contract awardees and their maximum potential values, inclusive of all future options, are: Astranis Space Technologies Corp. for $264.3 million; Global Enterprise Solutions Inc. for $340.4 million; and Viasat Inc. for $460.9 million. These contracts are facilitated through NASA’s SCaN (Space Communications and Navigation) program’s Communications Services Project.

The work supports NASA’s decision to gradually retire the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite fleet and adopt commercial services for future missions. Ka‑band services are also required to support select in‑orbit missions that cannot feasibly modify flight hardware or transition to non‑compatible commercial services. For additional information, visit https://go.Nasa.gov/4iVfeVB.
summary: NASA awards Ka-band satellite relay contracts to Astranis, Global Enterprise, Viasat.

title: Laura Bohn discovers opioid alternative SR‑17018 that avoids respiratory depression
content:
Laura Bohn, senior associate vice president of research at University of South Florida Health, was tasked in 2012 with finding safer pain‑management drugs as the opioid crisis shifted from prescription pills to heroin. The National Institute on Drug Abuse funded her work.

In 2017 Bohn and colleagues published in the journal Cell that several compounds, including a promising one named SR‑17018, could relieve pain in mice without causing respiratory depression—a common cause of opioid‑related death. The study highlighted SR‑17018’s potential to reduce pain without the life‑threatening breathing suppression seen with many opioids.

The team filed a patent on SR‑17018 and discovered that mice treated with the chemical did not develop a high tolerance. Additionally, mice already dependent on morphine could consume SR‑17018 to reset their tolerance without experiencing painful withdrawal symptoms.
summary: Laura Bohn discovers opioid alternative SR‑17018 that avoids respiratory depression.

title: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist
content:
Binance announced that a group of hackers, identified by the FBI and TRM Security as North Korean actors, carried out a theft that targeted $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency from its wallets. The attackers used social‑engineering tactics and novel malware, and the operation began no later than June, continuing until last Thursday when they successfully compromised an engineer’s laptop and withdrew assets from several wallets.

The exchange reports that it has frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of the stolen amount. Binance has set aside the funds necessary to cover the loss and has linked to a Proof of Reserves page to demonstrate its financial position. The $6.34 billion figure represents the largest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft.

Binance described the threat actors as sophisticated and resourceful, noting that the heist was the result of months of planning and execution.
summary: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist.

title: Democrats' sweeping midterm win called “once‑in‑a‑generation” repudiation of Trump
content:
Erin Ogunkeye welcomed Adam Jentleson, President of the Searchlight Institute and author of Supermajority: How Democrats Can Build Lasting Power, to discuss the recent midterm election.  

Jentleson said the Democrats’ sweeping victory is “more than the familiar backlash against an incumbent president.” He described it as a “once‑in‑a‑generation event” that signals a historic repudiation of Trump and the MAGA movement.  

The president noted that the electoral breadth of the win creates a governing dilemma. He asked whether a coalition that includes progressive reformers and culturally conservative Democrats can translate its diversity into legislative action. “Pluralism is not just a political strategy. It is actually a moral good in a democracy,” he insisted.  

Jentleson also questioned whether a party united by opposition to Trump can maintain that unity when faced with difficult choices on healthcare, immigration, economic inequality, and climate change.
summary: Adam Jentleson, president of the Searchlight Institute, said the Democrats' sweeping midterm victory is a once‑in‑a‑generation repudiation of Trump and the MAGA movement. He cautioned that the party’s broad coalition of progressive reformers and culturally conservative Democrats may struggle to turn its diversity into legislative action.

content: Even Trump seems to recognize that the relationship has become a political liability, and may never be the same On the eve of a midterm election that ended in an unequivocal rejection of his brand of politics, even Donald Trump seemed to recognize that the US-Israel relationship had become a political liability. content:
A high‑speed train operated by Spain’s state‑owned rail company Renfe collided with the rear of a stationary train run by private operator Iryo at 8:53 a.m. on Wednesday near the town of Urda in Castilla‑La Mancha. The crash killed 69 people and injured more than 100, further eroding public confidence in the country’s rail network.

Pedro Sánchez and his socialist‑led coalition government are now racing to rebuild that confidence ahead of a snap election, a task described as immense. The recent accident adds to a pattern of deadly train crashes that have already left Spain’s rail system’s reputation depleted.

title: Italian director Tinto Brass, known for Caligula, dies at 93
content:
Italian film director Tinto Brass, who began his career as an assistant to Roberto Rossellini, died at the age of 93.  

He moved into sex films, believing “eroticism to be a fundamental key to human expression” and was known as a maestro of Euro erotica.  

Brass was once hailed as the “Antonioni of the 70s” and became known for bringing Italian erotic cinema to a wider audience with films such as Caligula and Salon Kitty.  

His wife Caterina Varzi and children Bonifacio and Beatrice Brass announced the news to the Italian press agency Ansa on Wednesday.
summary: Tinto Brass, an Italian film director famous for erotic movies such as Caligula and Salon Kitty, died at age 93. His wife Caterina Varzi and children Bonifacio and Beatrice Brass announced his death to the Italian press agency Ansa on Wednesday.

title: Serbia detains nine police officers and one former officer over alleged force on protesters
content:

The ministry added that the suspects allegedly tortured and intimidated protesters who were held in a garage of a government compound.

The protests, which swept Serbia, an EU membership candidate, in 2025 and 2026, followed a 1 November 2024 incident in Novi Sad where a concrete canopy collapsed at a renovated railway station, killing 16 people.
summary: Serbia detains nine police officers and one former officer over alleged force on protesters.

content:
A British healthcare worker who tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is being evacuated to the United Kingdom for treatment. The patient is in stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist “high consequence” infectious disease unit upon arrival.

title: Ramayana: Rise of a Legend Review: Nitesh Tiwari’s Epic Stars Ranbir Kapoor
content:
Nitesh Tiwari’s three-hour film, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, is described as India’s most expensive production to date and the first half of a larger epic. The movie adapts the ancient classical poem concerning Rama, the avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu, into a spectacular Indian melodrama featuring music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman. While the story has been adapted for screen in the past, this version is noted for its unprecedented scale and lacks musical numbers.

The narrative follows Rama, portrayed by Ranbir Kapoor, as a noble warrior and statesman in the city-state of Ayodhya. His destiny involves confronting Ravana, played by Naveen “Yash” Kumar, the king of Lanka. The source details that Ravana’s backstory includes a period of slavery that led him to pray for justice, resulting in Lord Brahma granting him superhuman athletic strength and indifference to pain. The film is characterized as a thoroughly engaging and rousing blockbuster that appeals to audiences seeking a grand, Shakespearean-style tale of duty and war.
summary: The three-hour film directed by Nitesh Tiwari features music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman. Ranbir Kapoor plays Rama in this first-half blockbuster based on the ancient classical poem.

title: Review: Amazon's The Greatest retells Muhammad Ali's well-known life
content:
Amazon’s new limited series, The Greatest, offers a straightforward retelling of Muhammad Ali’s life, aiming to introduce the boxing icon to younger generations. The Prime Video drama is described as the first-ever “authorized scripted series” about Ali and features his widow, Lonnie, as an executive producer. While the show claims to be based on Ali’s life, it primarily takes its direction from a definitive book authored by his younger brother, Rahaman Ali.

Rahaman Ali, who served as a lifelong sparring partner and prominent member of the champion’s entourage until his death in 2016, provides the narrative foundation for the adaptation. The series covers well-known aspects of Ali’s biography, including his rise in boxing, his exile from the sport for refusing the draft, his late-career comeback, and his resilience following a Parkinson’s diagnosis.

Critics note that while the show offers small pleasures, it lacks novelty for most viewers. The review suggests that the adaptation repackages a story told too many times, reflecting a viewing public with diminishing patience for source material. The series is characterized as sturdy but ultimately unoriginal, relying on the cultural ubiquity of Ali’s public figure status to justify its existence.
summary: The Amazon Prime Video limited series The Greatest repackages Muhammad Ali's life, drawing heavily on the definitive book by his brother Rahaman Ali. The show serves as the first authorized scripted series about the boxer and features his widow Lonnie as an executive producer.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Patrick Stewart remembered by readers for RSC roles and community support
content: From coaching youth community theatre to supporting Huddersfield football club and delighting sci-fi fans at graduation ceremonies, the actor is fondly remembered Patrick Stewart – a life in pictures On Star Trek, Patrick Stewart could make anyone feel hopeful for humanity Patrick Stewart brought gravitas and complexity to the screen ‘He stood for the best of us’: William Shatner and more pay tribute What I always loved about Patrick was that he genuinely seemed connected to where he came from despite his global success. Once a Yorkshireman, always a Yorkshireman. I was lucky enough to see him at the Royal Shakespeare Company performing Hamlet, Merchant of Venice, and in Godot at the Haymarket, which is the only time the play has been so brilliantly performed as to make sense to me. I loved that he supported causes he clearly believed in, such as tackling domestic violence. He remained a good old-fashioned socialist. Got to applaud that. Shirley, 55, West Yorkshire

content:

Cadillac entered Formula One this year as a joint venture between General Motors and Walter’s TWG Global. TWG Global recently sold its controlling interest in the NBA’s Los Angeles Lakers and a 13% stake in Chelsea, and is currently exploring the sale of the WNBA’s Los Angeles Sparks.

content:

title: James Milner beats Muzzy Izzet for fastest footballer marathon time
content: Plus: managers sacked after signing new deals, war victims commemorated on kits and the first club website (part II) Mail us with all of your questions and answers It came as no surprise to the Knowledge that James Milner had spent the early months of his retirement training for – and then running in – the New York City Marathon. Yes, the bleep test-loving former Brighton, Liverpool and Manchester City player recorded an excellent time of 3hr 9min 4sec, an average of 7min 13sec per mile. Not bad for a 40-year-old whose physique is more like that of a wrestler than a whippet. “A few years ago, I feel like I could have definitely done sub-3:00,” he said, lamenting his late-career injuries for hindering him. In 2012 we ran a column listing footballers’ fastest marathon times, with the former Leicester playmaker Muzzy Izzet leading the pack on 3hr 22min 36sec at the 2011 London Marathon. That very respectable time has now been surpassed by the Premier League’s record appearance maker, so we thought we had better take a gulp of our isotonic energy drink and run through a few more tales of football’s marathon men and women.
summary: James Milner recorded a time of 3 hours 9 minutes 4 seconds at the New York City Marathon, surpassing Muzzy Izzet's previous record of 3 hours 22 minutes 36 seconds. This achievement makes the former Brighton, Liverpool, and Manchester City player the fastest marathoner among footballers.

title: Qatar withdraws from hosting 2028 Nations Championship finals
content:
Qatar has withdrawn from hosting the 2028 Nations Championship finals due to uncertainty stemming from the war in the Middle East. This decision also resulted in the cancellation of a planned title sponsorship deal with Qatar Airways. Following months of negotiations, both parties agreed to terminate an agreement that would have seen Qatar stage the six-match final series in 2028 and 2032, alongside a title sponsorship for four editions of the competition.

Paris’s Stade de France is now the most likely venue for the 2028 finals. The cancellation of the sponsorship arrangement with the national airline was part of the broader agreement to withdraw from the hosting and sponsorship commitments.
summary: Qatar will not host the 2028 Nations Championship finals due to uncertainty caused by the war in the Middle East. This decision also led to the cancellation of a planned title sponsorship deal with Qatar Airways.

content:

content:

title: Flint scientist Dr Siddhartha Roy wins 2026 Maddox Prize
content:
Dr. Siddhartha Roy, a third-year PhD student during the Flint, Michigan, water crisis, was part of a scientific team that publicly contradicted state and federal assertions that the lead-contaminated water was safe. This stance initially established him as a local hero. However, his reputation shifted after new research challenged the notion that children in Flint had suffered permanent brain damage from the crisis.

Roy’s commitment to adhering to the evidence, regardless of the resulting offense, has led to him receiving the 2026 Maddox prize. This award recognizes individuals who champion science and evidence in the face of challenges or hostility. In an interview with Ian Sample, Roy discusses his reflections on the Flint experience and notes that his work in the area caused him to lose friends.
summary: Dr Siddhartha Roy, a former PhD student, won the 2026 Maddox Prize for standing up for science during the Flint water crisis. He initially became a local hero for contradicting claims that the water was safe, but later faced criticism when new research challenged findings on permanent brain damage in children.

title: UN report finds rich nations' climate adaptation funding lags behind needs
content:
A United Nations report has found that financial support pledged by wealthy nations for climate‑adaptation measures in poorer countries has stalled. According to the report, flows of money to help vulnerable states cope with the climate crisis have been flat or even falling since 2022, even as extreme weather events increase and scientists warn that global warming may be accelerating.

The report details that adaptation funding—intended for stronger infrastructure, early warning systems, flood protection and drought‑resilient irrigation—remains woefully short of what is required. It also notes that the assistance is far below the promises made by rich countries in 2021, which themselves were already considered inadequate given those nations’ greater responsibility for the crisis.
summary: The UN report says financial support promised by rich nations for climate adaptation is far below what is needed. Flows of money to help poor countries have been flat or falling since 2022, even as extreme weather impacts grow and scientists warn global heating may be accelerating.

title: UK campaigners push for firework noise limit cut to 90dB to protect wildlife
content:
Campaigners are urging the UK government to lower the maximum noise limit for public fireworks from 120 to 90 decibels to protect wild animal welfare. The Center for Wild Animal Welfare (CWAW) argues this reduction is necessary to ease acute stress on birds and other animals. They contend that a 90dB limit, which is approximately one-eighth as loud as 120dB, would significantly reduce the area disturbed by fireworks, thereby safeguarding millions of wild animals.

The organization is pushing ministers to go beyond the previously proposed cut to 110 decibels. CWAW states that the more drastic reduction to 90 decibels would better address the acute stress caused to wildlife, ensuring a more substantial protection for animals affected by firework displays.
summary: UK campaigners push for firework noise limit cut to 90dB to protect wildlife.

title: Neurons in hippocampus separate location, timing, unfolding of experiences
content:
Neurons in the hippocampus help people separate different aspects of experiences. When recalling an experience, people often remember not only its location but also its timing and how it unfolded over time.  

This ability to recall sequences of events and associations helps guide actions in new scenarios.
summary: Neurons in the hippocampus separate different aspects of experiences. When remembering an experience, people recall where it happened, its timing, and how it unfolded over time, which helps them recall sequences of events and associations that guide their actions in new scenarios.

title: Age Influences Psychedelic Use's Link to Anxiety and Depression, Durham Study Finds
content: Age may influence the relationship between psychedelic use and mental health, according to new research from the Department of Psychology at Durham University. The study found that adults who had used classic psychedelics—such as psilocybin (magic mushrooms) and LSD—reported lower levels of anxiety and depression compared with nonusers, but this effect was limited to younger age groups. As age increased, the associations weakened and were no longer evident among older adults.
summary: Researchers from the Department of Psychology at Durham University found that adults with a history of using classic psychedelics such as psilocybin and LSD reported lower levels of anxiety and depression than nonusers. The association became weaker with increasing age and was no longer evident among older adults.

content: A recent study published in the September 2026 issue of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Diseases: Journal of the COPD Foundation suggests that a diet rich in red, yellow, and orange fruits and vegetables may reduce inflammation and exacerbations in people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The research indicates that consuming colorful produce could help manage COPD‑related flare‑ups.
summary: A new study in the September 2026 issue of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Diseases: Journal of the COPD Foundation found that eating a diet rich in red, yellow and orange fruits and vegetables may help reduce inflammation associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). content:
A research team led by Professor Ji-Woong Choi of the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at DGIST has developed NONOS, a deep learning-based analysis technology. This tool precisely separates rhythms from underlying background signals in brain signals with high temporal resolution. The project involved collaboration with research teams led by Professor Han-Joon Kim of Kumoh National Institute of Technology, Professor Kyong Hwan Jin of Korea University, and Dr. Jong-Cheol Rah of the Korea Brain Research Institute.

title: Wild Animals Self-Deploy GPS Collars Using New Capture-Free Telemetry
content:
Wildlife researchers have traditionally needed to capture animals to attach tracking devices, a process that has posed challenges for six decades. A new approach developed at the Norwegian University of Life Sciences (NMBU) allows GPS collars to be deployed autonomously on free-roaming terrestrial wildlife. This technique, known as Capture-Free Telemetry (CFT), places tracking devices on wild animals as they interact with baited deployment units in their natural habitat.

The proof-of-concept study, published in BioScience, demonstrates the feasibility of this self-collaring method. By eliminating the need for physical capture, the approach offers a new way to study wild animals using GPS technology.
summary: Researchers have long struggled to attach GPS collars to wild animals because they must be captured. A new method from the Norwegian University of Life Sciences, called Capture‑Free Telemetry, lets animals self‑deploy GPS collars by interacting with baited units in the wild, as shown in a study published in BioScience.

title: One Third of Infants with Peanut Allergy Outgrow It Within First Year
content:
A recent study published in The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice reports that more than a third of infants previously diagnosed with peanut allergy no longer react to peanuts during subsequent testing. The research, conducted by the Murdoch Children’s Research Institute in Melbourne, involved 778 babies who had been diagnosed with peanut allergy and then underwent an oral food challenge. In the challenge, infants were given gradually increasing doses of peanut flour up to 2,500 milligrams—equivalent to two teaspoons of peanut butter—under medical supervision. The study found that 35 percent of the babies did not react to any dose, despite having shown rashes, swelling, hives, or other allergic symptoms after consuming peanut-containing foods and having skin prick or blood test results consistent with a peanut allergy.

The oral food challenge was carried out before the national oral immunotherapy programme, which has been offered free to all Australian babies diagnosed with peanut allergy under 12 months of age since 2024. The programme, overseen by ten public children’s hospitals, involves feeding small but gradually increasing doses of peanut flour over two years to desensitise infants. Parents of the 35 percent who passed the challenge were informed that their child was no longer considered to have a peanut allergy, could safely reintroduce peanut at home, and did not need to begin the immunotherapy programme.

The average time between initial diagnosis and the oral food challenge was six months, leaving unclear why a third of infants stopped reacting to peanut in such a short period. Dr. Tim Brettig, the medical lead of the programme, suggested that the infants may have had a transient allergy, where the immune system initially reacts aberrantly to a food but the response does not persist. Previous research has shown that roughly a third of children with peanut allergies naturally grow out of them by age six, but this is the first time a high proportion of peanut allergies have been found to resolve on their own in infants.

The findings have implications for how peanut allergy is diagnosed and managed. Dr. John Ziegler of the University of New South Wales noted that peanut allergy is often diagnosed based on clinical history and skin prick or blood tests without an oral food challenge. Routinely conducting oral food challenges could identify infants who do not need treatment and be cost‑effective. He emphasized that the study confirms the importance of confirming the diagnosis of peanut allergy before starting oral immunotherapy. The researchers caution that allergy treatments should only be conducted under medical supervision due to the risk of severe reactions such as anaphylaxis.
summary: In a study of 778 Australian infants previously diagnosed with peanut allergy, 35 per cent passed an oral food challenge and were found not to react to peanut flour. The findings suggest that a surprisingly high proportion of infants’ peanut allergies resolve within the first year, potentially eliminating the need for lifelong avoidance and treatment.

content: Scientists have discovered that applying a simple mechanical squeeze to altermagnets significantly alters their magnetic properties and electrical behavior. This breakthrough could facilitate the development of faster, more energy-efficient electronics and new technologies for quantum computing.

title: Scientists suggest cross-wiring of brain and body began in ancient fish visual systems
content: Scientists propose that the brain’s cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, likely originated over 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. This arrangement may not have evolved for a specific advantage but rather represents a legacy of evolution constructing new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

content: A new study warns that permanent daylight saving time could force American children to make at least 2 billion additional school commutes in darkness. Researchers found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely during dark mornings as after sunrise, potentially increasing safety risks and disrupting biological clocks.
summary: A new study warns that permanent daylight saving time could force American children to make at least 2 billion additional school commutes in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks and disrupting their biological clocks. title: Stanford researchers discover molecule that suppresses appetite and promotes weight loss
content:
Stanford researchers discovered an AI‑identified natural molecule that suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, offering a potential Ozempic‑like weight‑loss treatment without the common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss.

The molecule, called BRP, reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful.

content: Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle‑repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed “Super HGF,” more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age‑related chemical damage. Early mouse experiments support the breakthrough, which could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age.
summary: Scientists discovered a compound that turns a natural muscle‑repair protein into a more powerful version called 'Super HGF'. Early mouse experiments show the compound more than doubles the protein's ability to bind to a key receptor and protects it from age‑related chemical damage, potentially helping combat muscle loss as people age.

content: MIT scientists have overturned a two‑decade rule by showing that flexible molecular connections, rather than rigid ones, can unlock entirely new arrangements of nanoparticles. This discovery challenges conventional thinking about nanoparticle assembly. The breakthrough could enable a new generation of designer materials with unusual properties, potentially impacting electronics, medicine, and energy applications.

title: NASA looks for private companies to boost Hubble into higher orbit
content:
NASA is exploring a plan to prevent the Hubble Space Telescope from falling into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of operation, the telescope is losing altitude and could reenter the atmosphere as early as 2033 or 2034 without intervention.

To extend Hubble's operational life, NASA is soliciting proposals from private space companies. These firms are asked to suggest innovative methods to boost the observatory into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission concludes.
summary: NASA is exploring a plan to keep the Hubble Space Telescope from falling back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. The agency is asking private space companies to propose ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission ends.

title: SLAC scientists confirm third type of magnetism, altermagnetism
content:
SLAC scientists have confirmed the existence of a third type of magnetism, known as altermagnetism, challenging the nearly 90-year belief that magnetism consists of only two categories. By utilizing specialized X-rays, the researchers identified a unique magnetic signature that distinguishes these materials from conventional magnets.

Altermagnets offer a combination of stability and efficient information carrying, which could address significant limitations in current electronics. This discovery holds potential for developing faster computers, more efficient data centers, and advancements in quantum technology.
summary: Researchers at SLAC used specialized X-rays to discover a unique magnetic signature that confirms the existence of a third type of magnetism, altermagnetism. Altermagnets are stable and can efficiently carry information, offering potential improvements for electronics, data centers, and quantum technology.

title: Very good boys? The dark, dystopian rise of robot dogs | Arwa Mahwadi
content:
Arwa Mahwadi’s article explores the expanding role of robot dogs in the United States, contrasting their potential utility with concerns over their military and law enforcement applications. The piece highlights the purchase of mechanical canines by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the development of "mutant mutts" by a startup named Warhound. These developments prompt questions about the nature of these machines, which lack fur and faces but contain technology such as shoulder chips.

In San Francisco, a startup called Dimensional is paying individuals $20 (£15) an hour to walk four-legged robot dogs. This initiative is not for exercise but to generate training data for the company. As reported by the New York Times, the objective is to create operating systems that integrate with AI agents, enabling the machines to act more independently.

While the specific future actions of these autonomous robots remain undefined, Dimensional’s founder asserts that the technology will assist people. One cited example is the potential for the robots to carry groceries, a task the author notes their small chihuahua-mix cannot perform.
summary: Pups that carry your shopping are one thing – but what about the mechanical canines being bought up in the US by ICE? Or the mutant mutts due to be developed by a startup called Warhound?
